sysd-blocks-001.title: Caching: answering from a copy instead of the source
sysd-blocks-001.text:
The fastest way to answer a request is to have answered it already. A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data so that future requests for it can be served faster. The stored data is either a copy of data kept elsewhere or the result of an earlier computation. A cache attacks latency, the wait for an answer, which is the subject of {{ref:sysd-found-087}}.

Think of a cache as a pool of entries. Each entry holds a copy of data from a backing store, the slower place where the data really lives, plus a tag that says which data it copies. A client checks the cache first and uses the entry whose tag matches. A match is a cache hit. No match is a cache miss, and then the client must make a more expensive trip to the backing store. The data is typically copied into the cache on the way back.

A hit is faster than recomputing the result or reading a slower data store, so the more requests the cache serves, the faster the system performs. Why not make the cache enormous? Larger capacity means greater physical distances for signals, and so propagation delays. Fast technologies such as SRAM also cost more than commodity DRAM, flash or hard disks. To be cost-effective, caches must stay relatively small. They still work well because typical applications access data with a high degree of locality, a habit explained in {{ref:sysd-blocks-002}}.

CPUs and storage drives often include hardware-based caches, while web browsers and web servers commonly rely on software caching.

sysd-blocks-002.title: Locality of reference: why caches usually win
sysd-blocks-002.text: A cache is a bet that the future will resemble the recent past, and programs usually let it win. Locality of reference is the tendency of a processor or application to access the same set of memory locations, or nearby ones, repeatedly over a short period. It comes in two basic types. Temporal locality is the reuse of specific data within a relatively small time, so a copy kept in faster memory cuts the latency of later references. Spatial locality is the use of data elements within relatively close storage locations, and sequential locality is a special case of it. Data enters a cache one cache line, a block of neighboring data, at a time, so touching one element brings a few neighbors in with it. Poor locality does the opposite and causes cache thrashing and cache pollution. Walking a matrix row by row matches how C stores it and uses the cache well. As matrices grow, non-sequential traversals cause far more cache misses and RAM accesses.

sysd-blocks-159.title: The CPU cache: tiny, costly memory beside the core
sysd-blocks-159.text: Main memory can be tens to hundreds of times slower than a small memory sitting next to the processor core. That small memory is the CPU cache, a hardware cache that reduces the average time or energy needed to access data from main memory. It is typically costly SRAM and holds copies of frequently used data in fixed-size cache lines, each stored with a tag naming its memory location. Larger caches hit more often but answer more slowly, so processors use levels. L1, the smallest and fastest, is checked first, then L2, and often a larger L3 shared among cores, before main memory.

sysd-blocks-003.title: Cache hit ratio: the number that judges a cache
sysd-blocks-003.text:
A cache is judged by two numbers. The hit ratio of a cache is how often a searched-for item is found in it, expressed as the percentage of accesses that are hits. The other number is latency, how long after a request the cache can return an item when there is a hit. The miss ratio is simply 1 minus the hit ratio.

The ratio is not a property of the cache alone, because it varies by application. Video and audio streaming often has a hit ratio near zero, since each bit of the stream is read once, used and never read or written again. That first read is called a compulsory miss. Worse, many cache algorithms, LRU in particular, let streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again. This is called cache pollution. LRU is covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-007}}. Even the replacement strategy is a compromise between hit rate and latency. Faster strategies track less usage information, and more efficient ones track more.

sysd-blocks-005.title: Eviction policies: what a full cache forgets
sysd-blocks-005.text: A full cache has to forget something. On a miss, some existing entry is typically removed to make room for the new data, and the heuristic that picks it is the replacement policy. Cache replacement policies, also called eviction policies, are the algorithms that decide which items a full cache discards. One policy, LRU, replaces the entry accessed less recently than any other. More sophisticated algorithms also take into account how often entries are used. LRU is covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-007}}. Every choice trades hit rate against latency: tracking more usage information improves the hit rate for a given cache size, while tracking less makes the policy faster. A policy may also weigh other factors, such as item size, the time needed to obtain the item and expiration. And if the cache is large enough, no discarding algorithm may be needed at all.

sysd-blocks-004.title: Cache write policies: when the backing store finds out
sysd-blocks-004.text:
Reading from a cache is simple. Writing raises a question: when does the backing store find out? A cache's write policy governs when a write made to the cache is propagated to the backing store. A write-miss policy governs whether data is loaded into the cache on a write miss.

There are two main write policies. Write-through performs every write synchronously to both the cache and the backing store. Write-back first writes only to the cache and postpones the write to the backing store until the modified content is about to be replaced by another cache block. That is more complex. The cache must track which locations were written over and mark them dirty, then write them back only on eviction, a process called a lazy write. A read miss in a write-back cache may need two trips to the backing store: one to write back dirty data, one to fetch the requested data.

On a write miss, write allocate, also called fetch on write, loads the missed location into the cache and then writes. No-write allocate, or write around, writes directly to the backing store and loads data only on read misses. The usual pairings follow the logic. A write-back cache typically uses write allocate, expecting later reads or writes of the same location to hit. A write-through cache uses no-write allocate, because later writes must still go to the backing store.

Write-through is common over unreliable networks, where the coherency protocol needed between several write-back caches is enormously complex. Whatever the policy, a cached copy can become stale, or out-of-date, when other entities change the backing store or other caches update their copies.

sysd-blocks-008.title: Least frequently used: when popularity outlives its use
sysd-blocks-008.text: An item that was popular once can outstay its welcome. Least frequently used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and discards the items used less often first. It resembles LRU, the subject of {{ref:sysd-blocks-007}}. The difference is that LFU stores how many times a block was accessed instead of how recently. The flaw is a long memory. An object that was accessed often and then becomes unpopular stays in an LFU cache for a long time. It blocks newer or less-popular objects from replacing it. LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA) adds a cache-age factor to the reference count, so such objects become eligible for replacement. It also reduces the cache pollution LFU causes when a cache is small. Least frequent recently used (LFRU) combines the benefits of LFU and LRU. It splits the cache into a protected privileged partition for popular content and an unprivileged partition.

sysd-blocks-007.title: Least recently used: the default eviction rule
sysd-blocks-007.text:
When Singh's case studies choose an eviction policy for a URL shortener, WhatsApp, Twitter, Netflix or Uber, they choose the same one each time: LRU. Least recently used (LRU) discards the least recently used items first. The idea is easy; the bookkeeping is not. LRU must track what was used and when, so it keeps age bits for cache lines and finds the least recently used line from those bits. Whenever a line is used, the age of the other lines changes.

The cost grows with the hardware. When a CPU cache lets a line sit in any of many slots, generally more than four ways, the cost becomes prohibitive. Designers then often use pseudo-LRU, which needs only one bit per cache item. Operating systems cannot afford LRU in the critical path because of its high overhead, so they commonly use Clock, an approximation of it. LRU is also a family of algorithms that includes 2Q and LRU/K.

sysd-blocks-158.title: Cache coherence: keeping copies in agreement
sysd-blocks-158.text: When several caches hold copies of the same data, one copy can change while the others never find out. Cache coherence is the uniformity of shared resource data that is stored in multiple local caches. In a coherent system every cached copy of a shared memory region is the same. Changes in any cache must reach the copies in peer caches, and writes to the same location must be sequenced. Snooping broadcasts every request to all processors: faster given enough bandwidth, but not scalable. Directory-based protocols send point-to-point messages through a common directory, with longer latency but much less bandwidth, which suits larger systems.

sysd-blocks-160.title: The page cache: free memory put to work
sysd-blocks-160.text: The operating system quietly spends any memory that programs are not using on a cache. A page cache, or disk cache, is a transparent cache in main memory. It holds pages that originate from a secondary storage device such as a hard disk or SSD. Because that memory is easily reclaimed, there is generally no performance penalty. Disk reads and writes are slow and random accesses need expensive seeks, so more main memory means more data cached and better performance. A write goes to the cached page, which is marked dirty and flushed to disk before it is freed.

sysd-blocks-015.title: Buffer versus cache: similar parts, different jobs
sysd-blocks-015.text: A buffer and a cache both hold data on its way somewhere, so they are easy to confuse. A cache reduces accesses to slower underlying storage for data transferred repeatedly. A buffer reduces the number of transfers of otherwise novel data between communicating processes. It spreads the overhead of several small transfers over fewer, larger ones. It can reduce the jitter of latency even when data is written once and read once. A cache also needs a possibly distributed coherency protocol to stay consistent with where the data resides, which strict buffering does not. Caching almost always involves some buffering, but strict buffering does not necessarily involve caching.

sysd-blocks-013.title: Prefetching: fetch it before anyone asks
sysd-blocks-013.text: Why wait for a request that is probably coming? Prefetching loads data into a cache ahead of time, guessing that the next chunk or two will soon be required. The plain alternative, demand paging, reads only the minimum on a read miss. That might be one page of virtual memory, often 4 KB, from disk into the disk cache in RAM. Anticipatory paging also prefetches the next chunk or two. It helps most when the first chunk is slow to read but the next few arrive in much shorter times, as with disk storage and DRAM. Done optimally, prediction can bypass the latency altogether.

sysd-blocks-022.title: Caching strategies: keeping a cache and its data in sync
sysd-blocks-022.text:
A cache and the data store behind it can drift apart. Caching strategies are the patterns for keeping them in sync, and they split by direction. For reads there are two. In the first, the application loads data into the cache itself, a pattern covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-023}}. In read-through, the cache itself loads data from the store when a read misses. For writes there are three: write-through, write-around and write-back. They are often combined. For example, write-around is often used together with that first read pattern to make sure the cache is up to date.

A write-through cache writes data to the cache and the store simultaneously. That gives fast retrieval and complete consistency between them, at the cost of higher latency for write operations. Write-around sends writes straight to permanent storage, bypassing the cache. That may reduce latency but increases cache misses, because the cache must read from the store on a miss. Applications that write and quickly re-read data pay with slower reads from back-end storage.

A write-back cache, also called write-behind, writes only to the caching layer and confirms the write as soon as it completes there. The cache then syncs the write to the store asynchronously. This reduces latency and gives high throughput for write-intensive applications, but it risks data loss if the caching layer crashes. Having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.

sysd-blocks-025.title: Distributed cache: memory pooled across machines
sysd-blocks-025.text:
A cache is usually limited to the memory of one machine, unless it borrows from others. A distributed cache pools the RAM of multiple networked computers into a single in-memory data store used as a data cache to provide fast access to data. It can grow beyond the memory limits of a single computer by linking many computers together. Its hosts can be co-located or spread over different geographical regions. A global cache is one kind: a single shared cache that all application nodes use. When data is missing, the cache itself finds it in the underlying data store.

Each cache key is assigned to a specific shard, also called a partition. A technique for spreading keys evenly across shards, even if some crash or become unavailable, is the subject of {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}. A common example is described in {{ref:sysd-blocks-029}}. The idea became feasible because main memory became cheap and network cards fast, with 1 Gbit standard and 10 Gbit gaining traction.

sysd-blocks-029.title: Redis: a cache that is also a data store
sysd-blocks-029.text:
Redis starts from a bold idea: a cache can also act as a full-fledged data store. Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory store of key-value pairs, used as a distributed cache and as a broker for messages. It serves reads and writes from main memory with sub-millisecond latency. It also persists data to disk with snapshots (RDB) and AOF, so it can serve as fully persistent storage.

Redis is fast for three reasons. It is RAM-based, and RAM access is at least 1000 times faster than random disk access. It uses IO multiplexing with a single-threaded execution loop. And it uses efficient lower-level data structures: strings, bitmaps, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes and JSON. These suit counting clicks and comments per post (hash) or sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set). Top use cases are distributed caching, session storage, passing messages and a high-speed store. The price is that Redis operates as a single process, so one instance cannot run tasks in parallel.

sysd-blocks-030.title: Memcached: servers that never talk to each other
sysd-blocks-030.text:
Memcached keeps its design simple enough that its servers never talk to each other. It is a general-purpose distributed memory-caching system. It often speeds up dynamic database-driven websites by caching data and objects in RAM, so an external data source is read less often. Servers keep a key-value associative array that clients populate and query by key. Keys can be up to 250 bytes and values at most 1 megabyte. Each client knows all the servers and hashes the key to pick one, a simple form of sharding. When memory runs out, servers discard the oldest values. Clients must therefore treat Memcached as a transitory cache and never assume stored data is still there.

In the usual read pattern the client checks for a value under a unique key, such as userrow plus the user id. If it is absent, the client selects from the data store and adds the result to Memcached. After an update, the cached view goes out of date unless the code also sets the new value or deletes the entry.

sysd-blocks-032.title: Redis replication and clustering: copies for reads, clusters for scale
sysd-blocks-032.text: One Redis server can feed any number of copies of itself. Redis scales reads and protects data through master-replica copying, and scales further through a clustering mode. A replica may itself be master to another, giving a single-rooted tree. The copies help reads and data safety but not writes, and replicas can be configured to accept writes, which permits inconsistency between instances. A Redis cluster can scale up to 1,000 nodes, achieve acceptable write safety and keep operating when some nodes fail. In a cluster all single-key commands are available, but multi-key operations are restricted to keys that belong to the same node.
